artifact.summary: The US data centre development pipeline expanded by 54 GW in the second quarter of 2026, marking a 29% increase year-on-year as developers accelerated construction amid growing concerns over power availability, according to a new report by Wood Mackenzie. The expansion is expected to intensify the focus on electricity supply, grid infrastructure and clean energy procurement as data centres emerge as a major source of incremental power demand in the US. The cumulative disclosed data centre pipeline has crossed 430 GW, with around 59% of the capacity under active development. Nearly 80 GW of projects were under construction, up from 44 GW at the end of the first quarter, Wood Mackenzie said in its US data centre pipeline report. The pipeline added 5% capacity quarter-on-quarter. Meanwhile, utility commitments backed by signed electricity service or construction agreements reached 201 GW, equivalent to 26% of projected US peak electricity demand in 2026. artifact.title: What Anthropic’s S-1 Reveals About Data Centers, Chips and Networking
artifact.summary: Anthropic’s newly filed Form S- 1 provides a detailed view of the physical infrastructure supporting Claude. Beyond the financial disclosures, the document describes an expanding compute strategy that combines hyperscale cloud services with dedicated accelerator capacity, creating growing requirements for data centers, power systems, semiconductors and high-capacity networks. The infrastructure story is particularly significant because Anthropic is not committing to a single chip architecture. Its operating model spans AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs and AMD GPUs, with capacity coordinated across providers. The S-1 also details approximately $161.2 billion in equipment lease payments associated with Broadcom-supplied TPU hardware over five years, excluding interest. For networking and data center suppliers, the filing points to a multiyear buildout in which facility commissioning, grid connections, thermal management and inter-data-center connectivity matter alongside the availability of AI accelerators. It does not, however, provide a definitive fiber-mileage forecast, optical transceiver procurement plan or annual megawatt deployment schedule. Google will indirectly pay Mid-Atlantic residents to reduce their power use when the grid is strained as a way to ensure enough energy remains available for the tech company's data centers. On Oct. 22, Google announced that Voltus, a virtual power plant company, agreed to provide Google with up to 1,070 megawatts of electric capacity as necessary for its data centers. To get that power, Voltus will give homes and businesses financial incentives to reduce their power demand when the grid is strained — or, to let Voltus reduce it for them. “Many of these reductions could occur automatically, such as through smart thermostats that dial back air-conditioning during peak summer hours or batteries that can provide temporary on-site power,” Brad Plumer writes for the New York Times. Voltus says that if thousands of businesses and homes agree, within a few years it can reliably provide Google with plenty of extra electricity when needed. While tech companies will likely need to continue investing in traditional power plants for their data centers, virtual power plants may offer a faster and more environmentally-friendly approach for the time being.
